introduction: This intermediate tier transitions to the dissolution of marriage and the welfare of children. It clarifies the legal distinction between Void and Voidable marriages, the grounds for divorce, and the rules of natural guardianship under the HMGA, 1956.

core_concepts.title: Void Marriages (Section 11, HMA)
core_concepts.description:
A Void marriage is *Void Ab Initio* (invalid from the very beginning, acting as if it never existed).
- Grounds: A marriage is void ONLY if it violates Section 5(i) [Bigamy], Section 5(iv) [Prohibited Degrees], or Section 5(v) [Sapinda Relationship].
- Legitimacy of Children: Even if a marriage is null and void, children born out of it are deemed **legitimate** under Section 16 of HMA and have rights to their parents' property.

core_concepts.title: Voidable Marriages (Section 12, HMA)
core_concepts.description:
A Voidable marriage is completely valid until one of the parties petitions the court to annul it.
- Grounds: (1) Non-consummation due to impotence, (2) Unsoundness of mind (violating Sec 5(ii)), (3) Consent obtained by force or fraud, (4) The respondent was pregnant by some person other than the petitioner at the time of marriage.

core_concepts.title: Theories of Divorce & Mutual Consent (Section 13, HMA)
core_concepts.description:
- Fault Theory (Sec 13(1)): Divorce based on wrongs like Adultery, Cruelty, Desertion, Conversion, or Insanity.
- Mutual Consent (Sec 13B): Introduced in 1976. Both parties agree to dissolve the marriage. Requirements: Living separately for 1 year, mutually agreed, and a 'cooling-off' period of 6 to 18 months.
- Irretrievable Breakdown: Not an explicit statutory ground in HMA. However, the Supreme Court in *Shilpa Sailesh v. Varun Sreenivasan (2023)* held it can use its inherent powers under **Article 142** to dissolve a completely dead marriage directly, waiving the cooling-off period.

core_concepts.title: Hindu Minority and Guardianship Act (HMGA), 1956
core_concepts.description:
Section 6 defines Natural Guardians:
- For a legitimate boy or unmarried girl: The father, and *after* him, the mother.
- For a child under 5 years: Custody shall ordinarily be with the mother.
- For an illegitimate child: The mother, and *after* her, the father.
- Section 13 (Paramount Consideration): The ultimate deciding factor in any guardianship dispute is the **Welfare of the Minor**.

important_entities.name: Restitution of Conjugal Rights (Section 9, HMA)
important_entities.key_fact: A remedy to save the marriage.
important_entities.significance: When either the husband or wife has, without reasonable excuse, withdrawn from the society of the other, the aggrieved party may apply for restitution (order to return). If the decree is not followed for 1 year, it becomes a ground for divorce under Section 13(1A).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In HMGA Section 6, the statute says the father is the natural guardian, and 'after him', the mother. In the landmark case *Githa Hariharan v. RBI (1999)*, the Supreme Court ruled that 'after him' does NOT mean only after his death. It means if the father is completely apathetic, physically absent, or unfit, the mother can act as the natural guardian even while the father is alive.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Void = Bigamy & Blood (Sapinda/Prohibited). Voidable = Mind, Force, Fraud, Pregnancy.
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Use this quick association to categorize the grounds for annulment.

exam_strategy_tips: If a question asks 'Are children of a void Hindu marriage considered illegitimate?', the answer is **NO**. Section 16 of the HMA confers legitimacy on them to protect innocent children from societal stigma.
